data.name: Smash Pixel Racing
data.detailed_description:
Smash Pixel Racing is a 2-4 player local multiplayer game about spaceship racing and smashing your friends into asteroids. Compete against friends in no-rules brutal spaceship racing and combat, or play cooperatively and see how long you can survive together.

Split second decisions and lightning reflexes will ensure your survival on the race to the finish line. No re-spawning, it's last man standing in space, survival of the fittest. If you make it to the finish line, you've earned it. Drift and dodge around space junk, take out enemies, collect energy, and pick your moment to boost, shoot or smash your way to victory!

Choose your spaceship and take it to victory! Ships are balanced but split into weight classes with different stats, find a ship that meets your play style!

Throughout Early Access we will be refining the game, adding lots of awesome content, new features & mechanics, many new ships to race, different enemies and obstacles, new game-modes and more so stay tuned!

2-4 Game-pads required (Windows Xbox game-pads recommended)
Smash Pixel Racing is local-multiplayer only!

reviews.review:
Smash Pixel Racing is a small-scale arcade racing game that mixes high-speed competition with spaceship combat, physics-driven collisions, and environmental hazards. Developed and published by Jollyfish Games, it approaches racing less as a test of perfect driving lines and more as a chaotic contest of survival. Players pilot compact spacecraft through hazardous courses while trying to maintain speed, avoid obstacles, collect useful energy, and interfere with their opponents. The concept is immediately understandable, but the addition of combat and physical collisions gives each race a more unpredictable character than a conventional arcade racer.

The central gameplay works because racing and fighting are closely connected rather than operating as separate systems. Players are encouraged to use their ships aggressively, whether that means shooting rivals or physically forcing them into dangerous objects. Asteroids and other environmental obstacles become potential weapons when a well-timed collision sends an opponent directly into trouble. This creates an enjoyable balance between controlling the spacecraft accurately and watching what the other racers are doing. Simply being the fastest pilot is not necessarily enough because an aggressive opponent can change the outcome through a successful attack or carefully positioned collision.

Energy management introduces another layer of decision-making. Energy gathered during play can be valuable for boosting and offensive actions, so players must choose when spending it offers the greatest advantage. Using resources aggressively may provide an opportunity to overtake or eliminate a rival, but wasting them can leave the player vulnerable later. Combined with health, weapons, enemies, obstacles, and physics-based impacts, this system gives the otherwise straightforward racing mechanics a welcome strategic element. The game remains accessible enough for a party setting while still giving experienced players opportunities to improve their timing and positioning.

Different spacecraft further support this competitive structure. The ships belong to different weight classes and possess varying characteristics while being designed around overall balance. These distinctions allow players to experiment with vehicles that better match their preferred approach. A lighter or more maneuverable craft may appeal to someone who concentrates on avoiding danger and navigating efficiently, while a heavier option can feel more appropriate for players who enjoy using physical contact aggressively. Because collisions are such an important part of the experience, differences in ship behavior can noticeably influence how players approach confrontations.

Smash Pixel Racing provides several modes built around the same fundamental mechanics. Race delivers the most recognizable objective, asking competitors to survive the course and reach the finish ahead of their rivals. Elimination shifts attention toward staying alive while opponents are removed from contention, making survival and aggression particularly important. Endless offers another variation for players who want to test themselves against continuing challenges. Survival can be played alone or cooperatively, providing an alternative to the competitive focus and allowing players to work together rather than constantly trying to destroy each other.

Multiplayer is where the game makes the strongest impression. It was fundamentally designed as a local multiplayer experience for two to four participants, making it best suited to a group gathered around the same computer. The frantic combination of racing and deliberate interference works naturally in this environment because much of the entertainment comes from unexpected mistakes, sudden attacks, and reactions between players. A rival who appears certain to win can be knocked into an obstacle moments before reaching safety, while an aggressive player can easily destroy their own chances by attempting an overly ambitious maneuver. These situations give the game the spontaneous humor expected from a good local party title.

There are significant accessibility limitations associated with that design. The original multiplayer setup relies heavily on gamepads, and the game was built around local rather than conventional online multiplayer. This means anyone approaching it as a traditional online racing game may find the structure restrictive. Its greatest appeal comes when the necessary controllers and players are readily available. Solo players have access to Survival, but the overall concept loses some of its personality without human opponents creating additional chaos.

The game's Early Access status is also impossible to overlook. Jollyfish Games originally presented an ambitious development roadmap that included more spacecraft, additional modes, graphical improvements, cooperative and team racing, new obstacles, more weapons, improved sound, additional events, and general polishing. The developer initially expected the Early Access period to last roughly six months. However, development did not progress according to that original timetable, and the project has remained in Early Access for many years without recent developer activity. As a result, the proposed future features should not be considered part of the current value of the game.

This lengthy period of inactivity is the largest concern surrounding Smash Pixel Racing. The underlying mechanics were already functional during its Early Access period, including ship controls, physics, collisions, combat, health, energy, enemies, and obstacles, so there is still a playable foundation. Nevertheless, the difference between the intended final product and the existing version is important. Anyone considering the game today should evaluate it strictly according to the content already available rather than expecting the original development plans to eventually be completed.

From a presentation standpoint, Smash Pixel Racing maintains a deliberately modest arcade identity. It does not attempt to compete with visually elaborate racing productions, instead concentrating on keeping ships, hazards, and action readable during hectic encounters. Its lightweight technical requirements also reflect the limited scope of the project. This simplicity can actually benefit local multiplayer because players can concentrate on reacting to what happens rather than learning complicated simulation mechanics or managing elaborate vehicle systems.

Ultimately, Smash Pixel Racing contains the foundation of an entertaining multiplayer party racer. Its combination of spaceship racing, weapons, energy management, hazards, and physics-based collisions creates plenty of opportunities for amusing competitive situations. The different modes and ship characteristics provide some variation, while the aggressive racing mechanics distinguish it from ordinary arcade racers. Unfortunately, limited content, dependence on local multiplayer conditions, controller requirements, and its long-standing Early Access situation prevent the promising concept from reaching its full potential. What remains is a straightforward and occasionally exciting multiplayer experience that works best when approached as a modest party game rather than a fully developed racing package.

Rating: 6/10
